title: Pringles or a Hyperbolic Paraboloid
body:
Pringles is the most famous stackable potato-based chip brand in the world. Almost everyone has enjoyed Pringles as a snack. But if you are a curious person, then you would have thought about its perfect shape and the fact that it’s so easy to stack the chips.

Pringles’s design is inspired by the mathematical geometry of Hyperbolic Paraboloids. Hyperbolic Paraboloids are also referred to as “saddles”. Its vertical cross-sections are Paraboloids and the horizontal cross-sections are Hyperbolas.

The above curve can be generated through a small python code (Github link)

Why the choice of a Hyperbolic Paraboloid as the shape?

The choice of a Hyperbolic Paraboloid as a shape is very unique and innovative. But there is strong reasoning behind this choice.

1. The double curvature of the Hyperbolic Paraboloid prevents stress concentration on the surface. This is the reason there is an extra crunch in Pringles.

2. This shape allows the chips to remain thin yet strong.

3. The saddle shape allows for easier stacking of chips and reduces chip cracking during transportation.

A lot of architecture designs are inspired by Hyperbolic Polaroids as they can be easily constructed from straight sections of materials. Some of these include London Velopark, England (2011), L’Oceanogràfic in Valencia, Spain (2003), etc.

So the next time you eat Pringles, reflect on the thought and effort that went into creating perfect, crispy chips.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Design of Experiments
body:
Being a data scientist, you will have to solve business problems with insufficient data. It will become tough for you to extract insights from the data to make decisions. In such cases, you will have to design a set of experiments for addressing the business case. Conducting a hypothesis test is your best bet. Let’s see how!

Hypothesis Testing

In layman’s words, hypothesis testing is an educated guess about a question someone has posed related to the data. Hypothesis testing is a statistical significance testing method to test how the results relate to the questions you are interested in addressing. The basic concepts that are a part of hypothesis testing are p-value, significance level, type I/II errors, minimal detectable effect, and power of the test.

Let’s start building a design of experiments with a simple example: How to test whether a coin is fair or not?

Coin Fairness

Let’s say that a factory manufacturing coins, want to test whether its machines are producing fair or biased coins. The shop floor manager flips 20 coins and gets 15 heads and 5 tails. He comes to you with these results and asks you to tell him if the coins being produced are fair or biased. The binomial distribution can be used to find the probability of the outcome.

From the above graph, you can see that the probability of getting 15 heads is 0.014. Next, we calculate what the chances are of obtaining an equally or less likely result (outcomes below the red line). The probability is 0.041. This calculated value is called the p-value. P-value is defined as the total probability of equally or less likely observation happening in the experiment.

Type I Error

Let’s do a statistical test for coin fairness. If we toss 1000 fair coins, 1000 times each, and plot all the p-values, we get the below plot. The p-values have a uniform distribution. Now if we pick a threshold of 0.05 (vertical red line), then there is a 5% chance that the fair coin is biased. Based on the below graph, ~60 coins are biased.

the selected threshold value is called a significance level. The Null hypothesis is accepted or rejected based on the significance level. This error is called type I error.

Design of Experiment

Let’s consider the case where don’t know if the coins are fair or biased. To answer this question we will have to create an experiment as follows:

Null Hypothesis: P(heads) = 0.5

Alternate Hypothesis: P(heads) != 0.5

To test the hypothesis we can experiment by tossing a coin 100 times, and counting the total number of heads. The binomial distribution of the experiment is shown in the image below.

If the significance level is set at 0.01, the number of observations below the red line will falsely conclude that a fair coin is biased. So, if we get less than 40 or greater than 60 heads, then a fair coin will be considered biased.

The next question comes is that how many flips are needed to conduct this experiment. Two parameters need to be calculated to estimate this count:

1. Z — Confidence level (z-value)

2. E — Maximum Error

This hypothesis testing approach is applicable to other business problems like detecting defective items, two party polling, etc.

Conclusion

I have tried to touch some basic concepts of hypothesis testing. You can do some more reading before working with Hypothesis Testing.
